storm.summary_layperson: Thunderstorms, some with strong cores, are closing in on the cove from the northwest, and unlike a typical summer evening there's no protective cooling effect from the Sound tonight to weaken them first.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air and Sound water are essentially the same temperature (75°F) right now, so the marine layer that normally shields the cove from incoming storms isn't in play tonight.
storm.detail_html:
A Flood Watch is in effect for the area, and an NWS Area Forecast Discussion issued this afternoon notes a Severe Thunderstorm Watch covering NE New Jersey and the Lower Hudson Valley, with an isolated damaging-wind threat possible into this evening. Instability is moderate-to-high (CAPE near 1,590 J/kg) but shear is weak (about 13 kt), which favors pulse-type storms with brief, isolated damaging gusts over a sustained severe line — the forecast discussion specifically calls out gusts above 40 kt as possible with any individual cell.

No protective mechanism is active at the cove tonight. The Sound-effect "bubble" that often weakens storms here depends on a stable marine layer, which needs a meaningful air-water temperature gap. Right now air and water are within 0.2°F of each other — there's no thermal contrast for a marine layer to form, so incoming storms should hit the cove with about the same intensity as surrounding towns.

Radar shows a cluster of cells 10–18 miles out to the WNW/NNW/NW, all tracking toward the cove. The nearest is a modest 36 dBZ cell about 10 miles out, but two or three cells behind it are considerably stronger — up to 58 dBZ — roughly 17–18 miles out and trailing by 30–40 minutes. Expect a first, weaker pulse followed by a more energetic second wave.

What would change the call: if the 45+ dBZ cells weaken or stall before closing the last several miles, or if reflectivity trends down on the next few radar scans, this would downgrade toward moderate. Conversely, if shear increases or the cells organize into a more contiguous line, that raises the severe-wind risk further.

The nearest cell's arrival window is 5:34–6:06 PM, medium confidence — radar-measured motion, but on a fairly distant, only moderately reflective cell. Because there's no marine layer today, don't expect the usual late-edge stretch or weakening the cove sometimes gets on hot, humid evenings; lean toward the window holding as forecast rather than running late.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 10 mi WNW closing at about 10 kt; with no marine layer to slow it down tonight, lean toward the early-to-on-time side of the window rather than expecting a stall.

wind.tactics_blurb: Moderate SSW gradient wind (10-12 kt) holds through the top of the window, but a cluster of thunderstorm cells (up to 58 dBZ) is closing from the WNW and likely crosses the cove between about 5:45 and 6:30 PM — stay off the water for that stretch regardless of how fair the breeze looks beforehand. Once it clears, expect gusty, backing wind settling toward light S/SSE for the rest of the evening.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day: the air-water temperature difference is only 0.2°F (75.2°F inland air vs. 75.0°F Sound water), far below the 5°F needed for a real thermal sea breeze, even though about 60% of coastal stations are currently reading southerly. That southerly flow is synoptic — warm-sector air ahead of the same disturbance producing tonight's storms — not a thermally-driven sea breeze. The gradient itself (airport-anemometer mean near 12 kt) sits in the moderate band.

S-SSW flow runs cleanly up the cove's north-south axis and is fairly uniform across the course, with maybe a touch more pressure near the mouth and east shore. No strong spatial edge to chase tonight — call the favored side center.

The shift character tonight is frontal/convective, not the gentle oscillation of a mature sea breeze (which wouldn't apply on a gradient day anyway). HRRR shows direction backing from S (170°) toward SSE (155-158°) over its next couple of forecast hours, while RYC right now is reading noticeably more veered at SSW 209° — a gap consistent with the approaching disturbance rather than any thermal effect. Expect the wind to back through S/SSE with a probable gust-front spike as the storm cells cross roughly 5:45-6:30 PM, then settle back toward light, steady S for the rest of the evening.

On the water: 10-12 kt SSW at the open is solid, powered-up dinghy conditions, easing toward drifter/light by 9-10 PM as the gradient relaxes. The real story tonight isn't the breeze — it's the storm risk crossing mid-window (see storm section); treat 5:45-6:30 PM as a no-go window.

HRRR only resolved 3 of its 12 forecast hours this cycle (f04-f12 failed to fetch), so the 20:00-22:00 numbers above are extrapolated from the observed backing/weakening trend rather than raw model output — treat them as lower confidence than the first three hours.
